title: Viking Tales
author: Jennie Hall
licenseEvidence: Project Gutenberg #24811: "Public domain in the USA"; title page reads "Copyright, 1902, By Jennie Hall" (Rand, McNally; published 1902)
description: Jennie Hall's classic 1902 read-aloud follows the Norse sagas from the boyhood of Harald Fairhair in Norway to the settling of Iceland and Greenland and Leif Ericsson's voyage to Wineland in North America. It is gentle enough for grades 2–4 and great for siblings together: read a short chapter or part, have your child tell it back, find the place on a map, and add it to a Viking timeline. The full text is free online.
includes: 25 lessons in 4 units, every chapter in order (long chapters split into parts)
Link to the exact page of the free full text for every lesson
Narration prompt, map work or drawing, and timeline date for each lesson
Parent notes on legend versus history, dated 1902 views, and violent or mature moments

units.title: Unit 1: The Sagas and Harald's Boyhood

lessons.title: What the Sagas Were
steps: Read the opening section, "What the Sagas Were," aloud together
Narration: tell how Iceland families spent long winter evenings and where the old stories came from
Map work: Find Iceland and Norway on a map; trace the sea between them with your finger
Timeline: Start a Viking timeline strip from 800 to 1050 AD; add "Sagas written down in Iceland" at c. 1200 AD
questions: What was a skald?
What did the people of Iceland write the sagas on?
Why did fathers tell these stories to their children?
answers: A man who sang or told the old stories, often with a harp
To make them brave and wise and teach them to love their country
lessons.notes: The sagas were written down in Iceland in the 1200s, two or three hundred years after the events in this book, so they mix real history with legend. The old vellum books are kept today in Reykjavik and Copenhagen as well as Norway.

lessons.title: The Baby
steps: Read "The Baby" aloud together
Narration: tell the queen's dream and how King Halfdan named his son
Map work: Find Norway and point to its long, jagged west coast full of fiords
Timeline: Add "Harald born" at c. 850 AD
questions: What did the queen see in her dream?
What name did the king give the baby?
What was the king's naming gift?
answers: A thorn that grew into a huge tree spreading over all Norway
lessons.notes: Harald Halfdansson is a real king, but stories of his birth, like the queen's dream, come from sagas written centuries later. Treat the dream as legend.

lessons.title: The Tooth Thrall
steps: Read "The Tooth Thrall" aloud together
Narration: tell what Harald and Olaf saw from the hill and the story of Aegir's Rock
Map work: On a map of Norway, find a fiord; draw a quick picture of a fiord with steep rock walls
Timeline: Add "Norse people worship Odin and Thor" across 800–1000 AD
questions: What is a thrall?
What did Olaf say made thunder and lightning?
What was the name of Odin's great feast hall?
answers: A servant who is not free (a slave)
lessons.notes: Thralls were enslaved people; Olaf wears an iron collar. The book treats this lightly, so talk about what it means. Aegir's leap is told as a brave deed in the Norse way of thinking; you may want to discuss it with sensitive children.

lessons.title: Olaf's Farm
steps: Read "Olaf's Farm" aloud together (it is a longer chapter; take a break halfway)
Narration: tell how Olaf built his dragon ship and how he spent a winter at the farmer's house
Map work: Find Denmark, Olaf's home, and trace a route across the water to Norway
Timeline: Add "Viking raids along the coasts" across 793–1066 AD
questions: What did Olaf name his ship?
How old was Olaf when he built his boat?
How did Olaf come to be Harald's thrall?
answers: He was captured, and the queen asked the king to spare him and give him to the baby
lessons.notes: Olaf tells raiding and taking over a family's farm as a merry joke. Ask your child how the farmer might have felt. This is a good chance to talk about how Viking raids looked to the people being raided.

lessons.title: Olaf's Fight With Havard
steps: Read "Olaf's Fight With Havard" aloud together
Narration: tell how Olaf's men escaped from the farmhouse
Draw: a Viking ship with its dragon head, sail, and oars
Timeline: Add "Viking ships sail the North Sea" at c. 800–900 AD
questions: How did Olaf's men find a way out of the house?
Why couldn't King Havard follow them by sea?
What did Olaf do to tease Havard as he sailed off?
answers: Thorkel fell against a panel and found a secret passage
Olaf's men had broken the oars of his ships and thrown the sails in the water
lessons.notes: This chapter has a fight in which a farmer is killed and men die. It is short and not graphic, but preview it for very young listeners.

lessons.title: Foes'-fear
steps: Read "Foes'-fear" aloud together
Narration: tell how Harald made his spear and what happened on the way home
Map work: Find France, Greece, Rome, and Arabia, places the things in Harald's home came from
Timeline: Add "Norse traders reach Constantinople and Baghdad" at c. 850–950 AD
questions: What did the runes on Harald's spear-point say?
What are skees?
What attacked Harald after he cut the spear handle?
lessons.notes: The Vikings really did trade far away; Arab silver coins and goods from Constantinople have been dug up in Scandinavia.

units.title: Unit 2: Harald, King of All Norway

lessons.title: Harald is King
steps: Read "Harald is King" aloud together
Narration: describe the funeral feast in the hall: the shields, the food, the mead-horns, the skald
Draw: a Norse feast hall with the fire down the middle and the high seats
Timeline: Add "Harald becomes king at age 10" at c. 860 AD
questions: How old was Harald when his father died?
Where did the men hang their shields at the feast?
Why did the skald get a bracelet?
answers: As thanks for his song about King Halfdan
lessons.notes: The sagas say Harald became king at ten; the exact year is uncertain (c. 858–860).

lessons.title: Harald's Battle
steps: Read "Harald's Battle" aloud together
Narration: tell how Harald called his men to war and how the battle field was marked
Map work: Find the inland valleys of southeastern Norway, where Harald's first kingdom lay
Timeline: Add "Harald's first battles for his kingdom" at c. 860s AD
questions: How did Harald call his men to war?
What did Thorstein raise on his spear to show he came in peace?
What did Harald do with the things taken from the enemy?
answers: He sent arrows from farm to farm
He divided them into piles for Thor, the king, the chiefs, and the men
lessons.notes: There is battle and burial of the dead here, told simply. The sacrifice to Thor shows Norse religion of the time.

lessons.title: Gyda's Saucy Message
steps: Read "Gyda's Saucy Message" aloud together
Narration: tell Gyda's message and the vow Harald made because of it
Map work: Compare Norway with Denmark and Sweden on a map; which were already one kingdom in the story?
Timeline: Add "Harald's vow to rule all Norway" at c. 865 AD (legend)
questions: Why wouldn't Gyda marry Harald at first?
What did Harald vow not to do until he was king of all Norway?
What new name did his uncle give him?
answers: He was king of too small a land; she wanted him to rule all of Norway
lessons.notes: The Gyda story comes from Snorri Sturluson's saga and is probably legend. The book says Harald's army burned houses as it went; a good place to ask how the common people felt.

lessons.title: The Sea Fight
steps: Read "The Sea Fight" aloud together
Narration: describe the ships and how the sea battle was fought
Draw: two lines of ships tied together prow to prow
Timeline: Add "Harald's great sea battles" at c. 870 AD
questions: Why did Arnvid's men tie their ships together?
What did the shield-guard on the high decks throw?
Who won the sea fight?
answers: So they could fight like one big floating battlefield, side by side
lessons.notes: Some warriors leap into the sea to die rather than surrender; the book presents this as brave. You may want to talk about it. The famous battle that finished Harald's conquest is called Hafrsfjord, traditionally dated 872.

lessons.title: King Harald's Wedding
steps: Read "King Harald's Wedding" aloud together
Narration: tell how Harald got his new name and what happened at the wedding
Map work: Trace Harald's kingdom: the whole coast of Norway from south to far north
Timeline: Add "Harald Fairhair king of all Norway" at c. 872 AD
questions: How many years did Harald fight before he cut his hair?
What new name did the earl give him?
What did Harald tie to Gyda's belt, and what did it mean?
answers: A bunch of keys; she was mistress of his house
lessons.notes: Historians today think Harald ruled mostly the western coast; "king of all Norway" is how the sagas remembered him.

lessons.title: King Harald Goes West-Over-Seas
steps: Read "King Harald Goes West-Over-Seas" aloud together
Narration: tell where the unhappy chiefs went and why Harald sailed west
Map work: Find Normandy in France, Ireland, Scotland, and the Orkney and Shetland Islands
Timeline: Add "Rollo (Rolf) gets Normandy" at 911 AD
questions: Why did many men leave Norway?
What did Rolf name his land in France?
How did people explain the queen's old dream at the end?
answers: They would not kneel to Harald or pay him taxes
Harald was the great tree; his kingdom and sons spread far like its branches
lessons.notes: Rolf (Rollo) got Normandy in 911. His descendant William the Conqueror became king of England in 1066, five generations later, so "his sons' sons" means great-great-great-grandsons.

lessons.title: Homes in Iceland, Part 1: The Vow
steps: Read pp. 103–109 of "Homes in Iceland" aloud, stopping after the night of the storm
Narration: tell why Ingolf and Leif decided to go to Iceland and what they packed
Map work: Trace a route from Norway to the Shetland Islands
Timeline: Add "Ingolf's first voyage to Iceland" at c. 870 AD
questions: Why did Ingolf and Leif need to leave Norway?
How many men did Ingolf take, and why only that many?
What happened to one man in the storm?
answers: They had killed two men and feared their kinsmen and King Harald
Thirty, one for each oar, because food and room were short
He was washed overboard and drowned
lessons.notes: This chapter is long, so it is split over five lessons. The sagas call Leif "Hjorleif" (Leif the Sword); he is a different man from Leif Ericsson later in the book.

lessons.title: Homes in Iceland, Part 2: Landfall
steps: Read pp. 110–117 aloud, from the rocky islands to the campfire talk under the northern lights
Narration: tell what strange things Ingolf found in Iceland
Map work: Find the Faroe Islands and Iceland; notice how the islands are like stepping-stones
Timeline: Add "Norse explorers reach Iceland" at c. 870 AD
questions: How long had they been at sea when they reached Iceland?
What did Ingolf think made the hot springs and rumbling ground?
What did Ingolf say the northern lights were?
answers: The flash of the Valkyrias' armor
lessons.notes: Iceland really does have volcanoes, geysers, hot springs, and glaciers. A short look at photos of geysers will help.

lessons.title: Homes in Iceland, Part 3: The High-Seat Pillars
steps: Read pp. 118–126 aloud, from the return to Norway through the long, gloomy winter
Narration: tell what Ingolf did with the pillars of his high seat and why
Hands-on: carve or draw a tall pillar decorated with dragons and Thor's hammer
Timeline: Add "Ingolf settles in Iceland" at 874 AD (traditional date)
questions: What did Ingolf bring from under the old altar?
Why did Ingolf throw the pillars overboard?
Why was Ingolf's wife sad at Yule-time?
answers: Earth (soil of Norway) in a little bronze chest
So Thor would guide them to the place where he should build his home
She missed the merry feasts and friends in Norway
lessons.notes: Ingolf sacrifices horses to Odin; this is how Norse religion worked, and the book describes it plainly. 874 is the date Icelanders traditionally give for the first settlement.

lessons.title: Homes in Iceland, Part 4: Reykjavik
steps: Read pp. 127–135 aloud, from the bad news about Leif to the games at the new home
Narration: tell what happened to Leif and how Ingolf finally found his pillars
Map work: Find Reykjavik and the Westman Islands off Iceland's south coast
Timeline: Add "Reykjavik founded" at c. 874 AD
questions: How long did Ingolf wait before his pillars were found?
What does Reykjavik mean, and why did Ingolf choose that name?
How did Ingolf claim the land?
answers: "Smoky sea" (smoky bay), because of the steaming hot springs
He built fires at the mouth of the rivers
lessons.notes: Leif is killed by the thralls he brought from Ireland, and Ingolf kills them in return. Preview this for sensitive listeners. The islands where the thralls hid are still called the Westman Islands ("Islands of the Westmen," meaning Irishmen).

lessons.title: Homes in Iceland, Part 5: The Father of Iceland
steps: Read pp. 136–142 aloud, to the end of the chapter
Narration: tell how Iceland changed by the time Ingolf was old and how he was buried
Draw: Ingolf's ship grave under its mound
Timeline: Add "Iceland's Althing (assembly) founded" at 930 AD
questions: Why were Ingolf and his men so happy to see a sail?
What did ships take from Iceland to Norway to sell?
What did people call Ingolf after he died?
answers: They had lived alone for years and were lonely for new faces and news
Cloth, wool, fish, oil, and bird feathers
lessons.notes: The burial includes killing horses and dogs to go with Ingolf to Valhalla. Ship burials like this are real; famous ones have been dug up in Norway (Oseberg, Gokstad). The book's note calling Reykjavik "the only city in Iceland" was true in 1902.

lessons.title: Eric the Red, Part 1: Outlawed
steps: Read pp. 143–150 of "Eric the Red" aloud, until they set off
Narration: tell why Eric had to leave Iceland and what land he wanted to find
Map work: Find western Iceland and look west across the sea toward Greenland
Timeline: Add "Eric the Red outlawed from Iceland" at c. 982 AD
questions: Why was Eric outlawed?
Who first told of the shining white land in the west?
Where did Eric and his men hide from Thorgest?
answers: He had killed men in his quarrels
In the woods and a secret cave at Eyjolf's farm
lessons.notes: Being "outlawed" meant Eric had to leave Iceland for three years, and anyone could harm him if he stayed.

lessons.title: Eric the Red, Part 2: Greenland
steps: Read pp. 151–160 aloud, to the end of the chapter
Narration: tell what Eric found on his voyage and why he chose the name Greenland
Map work: Find Greenland; notice the ice sheet in the middle and the green fiords on the southwest coast
Timeline: Add "Eric settles Greenland" at c. 985 AD
questions: What did Eric first think was one of Gunnbiorn's ships?
What did the men burn for fuel when there was no wood?
Why did Eric call the land Greenland?
answers: So people would like the sound of it and want to come
lessons.notes: The sagas say 25 ships set out and 14 arrived; this book says 35 and 15. The "strong river" in the sea is a real ocean current along Greenland's east coast. Eric's settlements lasted about 450 years.

lessons.title: Leif and His New Land, Part 1: King Olaf and a Strange Shore
steps: Read pp. 161–167 of "Leif and His New Land" aloud, until Leif goes to look for Tyrker
Narration: tell about Leif's visit to King Olaf and the storm that blew him to a new land
Map work: Trace Leif's path from Greenland to Norway, then follow the storm southwest toward North America
Timeline: Add "Leif Ericsson reaches North America" at c. 1000 AD
questions: Who was King Olaf related to?
What did King Olaf give Leif when he left?
What did the men like about the new land?
answers: He was the great-grandson of Harald Hairfair
The tall trees, soft grass, and rich black soil
lessons.notes: The sagas say King Olaf Tryggvason made Leif a Christian and sent him to bring Christianity to Greenland; this book leaves that out.

lessons.title: Leif and His New Land, Part 2: Wineland
steps: Read pp. 168–173 aloud, to the end of the chapter
Narration: tell what Tyrker found and what Leif brought home
Map work: Find Newfoundland in Canada, where a real Norse camp has been found
Timeline: Add "Leif names Wineland" at c. 1000 AD

links.label: Read "Leif and His New Land" from p. 168

questions: What had Tyrker found in the woods?
Why did Tyrker know what they were?
Why were the Greenlanders so pleased with the lumber?
answers: He grew up in Germany, where grapes grow everywhere
lessons.notes: Many experts think the "grapes" may have been other wild berries, or that the Norse reached farther south where wild grapes grow, beyond their camp in Newfoundland.

lessons.title: Wineland the Good, Part 1: Thorfinn and Gudrid
steps: Read pp. 174–179 of "Wineland the Good" aloud, until they decide to go
Narration: tell how Thorfinn helped Eric at Yule and why he wanted to sail to Wineland
Map work: Find Greenland again and trace a route south along the coast of Labrador
Timeline: Add "Thorfinn and Gudrid sail to Wineland" at c. 1010 AD
questions: Why was Eric gloomy before Yule?
How did Thorfinn solve Eric's problem?
Whom did Thorfinn marry?
answers: His storehouses were empty and he could not give his guests a good Yule feast
He gave Eric the flour, grain, and mead from his ship
lessons.notes: Gudrid (Gudrid Thorbjarnardottir) is one of the most traveled women of the Middle Ages; she later went on pilgrimage to Rome.

lessons.title: Wineland the Good, Part 2: The First Winelander
steps: Read pp. 180–184 aloud, until Snorri is born
Narration: tell how the settlers lived in Wineland and who was born there
Draw: the settlers' little huts by the lake with cloaks hung in the doorways
Timeline: Add "Snorri, first European child born in America" at c. 1010 AD
questions: How many men sailed to Wineland in three ships?
What did they use for doors on their huts?
What was the baby's name, and what did the men call him?
lessons.notes: Biarni says the land is empty, but people already lived there, as the next lesson shows.

lessons.title: Wineland the Good, Part 3: Strangers in Canoes
steps: Read pp. 185–193 aloud, to the end of the story
Narration: tell about the first meeting, the trading, and why the Norsemen went home
Map work: Find L'Anse aux Meadows on the northern tip of Newfoundland, Canada
Timeline: Add "Norse camp at L'Anse aux Meadows" at c. 1000–1020 AD; add "Columbus reaches America" at 1492 for comparison
questions: What did the strangers want to trade for?
What frightened the strangers away the first time?
Why did Thorfinn and his people leave Wineland?
answers: Thorfinn's bull came bellowing out of the woods
They were attacked and feared more people would come back
lessons.notes: The book calls the Native people "savages," "ugly," and "not men." These are prejudiced 1902 words; talk about how the people who already lived there would have seen the strangers. They were probably ancestors of First Nations such as the Beothuk or Mi'kmaq. The book says Wineland was on the eastern shore of the United States, but the only Norse site ever found (in 1960) is at L'Anse aux Meadows in Newfoundland, Canada.

lessons.title: Descriptive Notes: Norse Homes, Names, and Gods
steps: Read the Descriptive Notes at the back of the book (pp. 194–199) together
Narration: explain how names like "Ericsson" began and what a foster-brother was
Hands-on: make your own Norse name from your parent's first name (Annasdottir, Peterson) and a nickname
Timeline: Add "Viking Age ends" at 1066 AD and look back over your whole strip
questions: What does the name "Thorstein" mean?
What were peace-bands for?
What were the narrow slits high in a feast hall called?
answers: To tie a sword into its scabbard to show you came in peace
lessons.notes: The note on Eskimos repeats a 1902 guess that has since been disproved. The Inuit moved east from Alaska into Greenland around 1200, after Eric's settlers arrived; Eric found only ruins of earlier peoples. The "Suggestions to Teachers" and reading list that follow are for you, not the child.
